drivers.name: Price increase (6.2%) without promotion
drivers.evidence: Two prior weeks with same price: x0.70 and x1.29; pooled noise-adjusted estimate suggests x0.85. No promotion, so no lift. Past price hikes without promo reduce demand.

adjustment.analysis: The baseline median is 18.7. The target week has a 6.2% price increase to $12.03, above the regular $11.33. Past promotions show a median lift of x1.52 vs baseline, but noise-adjusted lift is x1.4. However, this week has no promotion—only a price increase. A prior week (2026-09-28) with the same price saw only x0.70 vs baseline (13 units), and 2026-10-05 (x1.29) also had no promotion. The noise-adjusted price effect is therefore likely negative. The classical uplift model shows no promotion effect, but we must adjust for price. Evidence from past price hikes (no promo) shows demand drops. The most relevant data: same price in 2026-09-28 (x0.70) and 2026-10-05 (x1.29). Pooled, this suggests a noise-adjusted price penalty of ~x0.85. Confidence is medium due to limited data. No event or promotion, so no uplift. Adjust downward.

brief:
PRODUCT: Cold & Flu Relief | category Health | Store #12 (Austin, TX)
TARGET WEEK: 2026-11-09 to 2026-11-15 (5 weeks after the last week with sales data)

KNOWN PLAN FOR THE TARGET WEEK:
  events: none
  shelf price: 12.03 (+6.2% vs regular price 11.33)

STATISTICAL BASELINE (exponential smoothing of recent sales; it ignores events, promotions and prices):
  median 18.7 | 5%-95%: 3.6 - 38.4 | 10%-90%: 7.5 - 34.0

In the evidence below, 'vs baseline' = actual units / what this same baseline predicted for that week.
It is the multiplier that would have been right, so it maps directly onto median_multiplier.
This product's ordinary weeks already swing about +/-46% around the baseline, so a past effect smaller than that, seen only a few times, is mostly noise. The
'noise-adjusted estimate' is the effect shrunk toward x1.0 for that noise and the number of sightings.
